Lab 13: Simple Linear Regression Part 1

Jason M. Klemm

2026-08-16

Task 1

The SPRUCE data is read in and the first \(6\) entries are provided as follows:

# Read in data
spruce <- readxl::read_xls("~/Desktop/OU_Masters/Summer_2026/MATH-4753G_Summer_2026/K25936_Downloads/K25936_Downloads/Excel/SPRUCE.XLS")
# Output the first 6 entries 
head(spruce, 6)
## # A tibble: 6 × 2
##   BHDiameter Height
##        <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1       18.9   20  
## 2       16.6   18.8
## 3       15.5   16.8
## 4       15.5   16.9
## 5       19.4   20.2
## 6       13.7   16.3

Task 2

Below is the plot for Height vs. BHDiameter:

# Make plot
spruce |> ggplot(aes(x = BHDiameter, y = Height)) +
  geom_point(colour = "navy") +
  labs(title = "Jason's Plot")

Task 3

Now taking the same plot from above and adding a LOESS line on it:

# Make plot with LOESS
spruce |> ggplot(aes(x = BHDiameter, y = Height)) +
  geom_point(colour = "navy") +
  labs(title = "Jason's Plot - loess") +
  stat_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y~x)

What I can conclude from the plot is that the relationship between BHDiameter and Height is positive. This meaning that as BHDiameter increases, Height also increases. As indicated by the ‘loess’ line this data supports a curve more than it does a line. In other words the relationship appears to be non-linear.

Task 4

Below is the output of the lm() of our SPRUCE data:

# Linear Model of SPRUCE Data
mod <- lm(Height ~ BHDiameter, data = spruce)

# Summary of mod
summary(mod)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Height ~ BHDiameter, data = spruce)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.9394 -0.9763  0.2829  0.9950  2.6644 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  9.14684    1.12131   8.157 1.63e-09 ***
## BHDiameter   0.48147    0.05967   8.069 2.09e-09 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 1.678 on 34 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.6569, Adjusted R-squared:  0.6468 
## F-statistic:  65.1 on 1 and 34 DF,  p-value: 2.089e-09

The equation for the linear model can be expressed as follows from the summary:

\[\widehat{\text{Height}} = 9.14684 + 0.48147(\text{BHDiameter})\]

Task 5

Going back to the plot from Task 2 we can add the line equation above as follows:

# Make plot with LOESS
spruce |> ggplot(aes(x = BHDiameter, y = Height)) +
  geom_point(colour = "navy") +
  labs(title = "Jason's Plot - lm") +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y~x)

Task 6

Below is the residuals vs fitted values plot:

# Data wrangling
new_spruce <- spruce |> mutate(residuals = lm(Height~BHDiameter)$residuals, yhat = lm(Height~BHDiameter)$fitted.values)

# Plot
new_spruce |> ggplot(aes(x = yhat, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(colour = "navy") +
  stat_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y~x) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values")

Part a

The problem that I see with the data given this plot and when compared to the assumptions of the SLR model is that it violates the first assumption which states \(\epsilon_i \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2)\). The diagnostic plot indicates that \(E(\epsilon)\) varies for every value of \(\hat{y}\) and does not randomly vary close to \(0\). Additionally we can see a clear non-linear pattern in the fitted line which would indicate that we have a misspecified model.

Part b

As stated above, the plot has a curved fitted line and indicates that we have a misspecified model in which the data likely has a quadratic relationship.

Task 7

Part a

The “as-is” operator must be added so that \(\text{BHDiameter}^2\) is evaluated as a whole before being added as a separate term of the regression model. It forces formula operators (i.e. “\(**\)”) in the formula to be interpreted as arithmetical operators.

Part b

Below is the quadratic regression model for the SPRUCE data:

# Quadratic model
qmod <- lm(Height ~ BHDiameter + I(BHDiameter**2), data = spruce)

# Summary of qmod
summary(qmod)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Height ~ BHDiameter + I(BHDiameter^2), data = spruce)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.2966 -0.6245 -0.0707  0.7442  3.2541 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)      0.860896   2.205022   0.390 0.698731    
## BHDiameter       1.469592   0.243786   6.028 8.88e-07 ***
## I(BHDiameter^2) -0.027457   0.006635  -4.138 0.000227 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 1.382 on 33 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.7741, Adjusted R-squared:  0.7604 
## F-statistic: 56.55 on 2 and 33 DF,  p-value: 2.182e-11

Task 8

Part a

When comparing only the adjusted \(R^2\) output between the regression models with and without the quadratic term, the model with the quadratic tern has an adjusted \(R^2 = 0.7604\) and the model without has an adjusted \(R^2 = 0.6468\). Therefore, the model with the quadratic term provides a better fit than without due it explaining a greater portion of the variance within the data as indicated by the adjusted \(R^2\) values.

Part b

The equation for the quadratic model can be expressed as follows from the summary:

\[\widehat{\text{Height}} = 0.860896 + 1.469592(\text{BHDiameter}) - 0.027457(\text{BHDiameter})^2\]
